summary: Seeing Jesus condemned, Judas returns the silver, confesses he betrayed innocent blood, and hangs himself; the priests buy a potter’s field, fulfilling prophecy.
key_insight: Judas said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” His confession was true, and he made it to the wrong people. The priests answered, “What is that to us?” He took his guilt to them instead of to the One he had betrayed.
story: That morning Judas, His betrayer, saw that Jesus had been condemned, and he was remorseful. He brought the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders and said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” They answered, “What is that to us? You see to it!”
Judas threw the pieces of silver down in the temple and left. Then he went and hanged himself.

The chief priests picked up the silver. “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury,” they said, “because they are the price of blood.” After consulting together, they used the money to buy the potter’s field as a place to bury strangers. That is why it has been called the Field of Blood to this day.

So the word spoken by Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the value of Him who was priced, whom they of the children of Israel priced, and gave them for the potter’s field, as the LORD directed me.”

Luke later adds more in the Book of Acts. The field was bought with the wages of iniquity, and Judas, falling headlong, burst open in the middle and all his entrails gushed out. Everyone in Jerusalem came to know it, so the field is called in their own language Akel Dama, that is, Field of Blood.
differences: Matthew says Judas hanged himself; Acts says that, falling headlong, he burst open.
Matthew says the chief priests bought the field; Acts says Judas “purchased a field with the wages of iniquity.”
Matthew says the field was called the Field of Blood because it was bought with blood money; Acts ties the name to Judas’s death there.

fit.question: Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field. Acts says Judas bought a field and died by falling headlong and bursting open. How do these fit?

points.label: Bought with his money
points.text: The priests made the purchase, but with Judas’s silver, money they would not take back as theirs. The field could fairly be called his purchase. Luke’s aside in Acts carries a hard irony: this is what his wages bought him.

points.label: Hanging, then falling
points.text: Matthew tells how Judas died; Acts tells what happened to his body. A body left hanging could fall when the rope or branch gave way and burst open on the rocks below. This explanation is very old, and nothing in either account rules it out.

points.label: Two reasons for one name
points.text: The field bought with blood money also became the place of Judas’s gruesome end. Matthew gives one reason for the name Field of Blood, Acts the other, and both could be true at once.

fit.note: Matthew and Luke each report a different part of what happened. Neither account excludes the other.
fit.short: Judas hanged himself, and his body later fell and burst open. The priests bought the field with his money, so it counted as his.

fit.question: Matthew says the prophecy was spoken by Jeremiah, but the words about thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter come from Zechariah 11:12–13. Did Matthew name the wrong prophet?

points.label: Two prophets, one fulfillment
points.text: The thirty pieces of silver and the potter come from Zechariah 11:12–13. But buying a field (Jeremiah 32:6–9), the potter (Jeremiah 18–19) and the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, renamed the Valley of Slaughter where the dead would be buried (Jeremiah 19:2, 6, 11), come from Jeremiah. Matthew blends the two and names the major prophet whose story supplies the field and the burial ground.

points.label: Why name Jeremiah
points.text: The point Matthew is explaining is the purchase of a burial field, and that is Jeremiah’s theme, not Zechariah’s. Older writers, including McGarvey, suggested a copyist’s slip, but the manuscripts strongly support “Jeremiah.”

fit.note: Matthew reads the Prophets as one voice. Drawing on two of them under the name of the leading one is a way of quoting, not a mistake.
fit.short: Matthew blends Zechariah’s thirty pieces of silver with Jeremiah’s potter and field, and names Jeremiah, whose story supplies the field.

scene.label: Remorse, not repentance
scene.text: Matthew’s word here is not his usual word for repentance (as in 3:2 and 4:17). It means regret, being sorry afterward. Paul draws the same line: “godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation,” but “the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

scene.label: Blood money
scene.text: The priests would not put money paid for blood into the temple treasury, much as the Law kept certain wages out of the house of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:18). They kept the rule about the coins after paying for the blood.

scene.label: The potter’s field
scene.text: This was probably land dug out for clay, poor for farming, and it became a cemetery for foreigners who died in Jerusalem, such as pilgrims at the feasts. Since at least the 300s, tradition has placed it on the south side of the Valley of Hinnom, where Jeremiah once broke a potter’s flask (Jeremiah 19).

scene.label: Akel Dama
scene.text: The name is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jerusalem, and means Field of Blood. Luke translates it for his Greek readers: “in their own language.”

scene.label: Another betrayer
scene.text: Ahithophel, King David’s trusted counselor, joined Absalom’s revolt against David. When his advice was rejected, he went home and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). He and Judas are the only two people in Scripture said to have hanged themselves.

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew among the Gospels tells the end of Judas. He sets it right after Jesus is condemned, so that the council’s verdict is answered at once by the man who betrayed Him: “innocent blood.” Matthew shows the chief priests refusing Judas’s confession and then fulfilling a prophecy they never meant to fulfill with the very silver they had paid him.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the innocent One. The man who sold Him said so, and even His enemies’ bargain fulfilled what God had spoken about the price set on His Shepherd (Zechariah 11:12–13).
seeing.living: Judas and Peter both failed Jesus that night, and both were sorry. Peter wept and was later restored; Judas took his regret to the priests and then to a rope. Sorrow over sin has to be taken to Jesus, the only One who can deal with it.
seeing.ponder: When you feel the weight of what you have done, where do you take it?

preaching.big_idea: Judas confessed that Jesus was innocent, but he took his guilt to the wrong place.
preaching.watch_for: “You see to it!” say the priests to Judas (v. 4). Pilate will throw the same words back at the crowd (27:24). In Matthew 27, everyone tries to push the blood of Jesus onto someone else.
